items.title: How Donald Trump warped the most important law protecting assault victims on campus
items.summary:
Protesters at a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe on October 13, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 

In the weeks since reports about an alleged gang rape at Cornell University went public, I’ve heard a lot of people ask why we haven’t made more progress on campus sexual assault. 

I understand the question. I started working on the issue as a student activist more than 15 years ago. Now, as an attorney at Public Justice, I represent student survivors of sexual assault in lawsuits against their schools. Seeing the stories out of Cornell sometimes makes me feel like nothing has changed since I was an undergraduate.

But that’s not quite right: We did make progress. Schools started taking more seriously their responsibilities to address sexual assaults, providing survivors with academic and mental health support to help them stay in school and setting up procedures to investigate allegations. This progress was spurred significantly by enforcement of Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex discrimination in education and offers protections to student survivors of sexual assault.

However, that progress was met by backlash — both political backlash specific to Title IX and a broader hostility to civil rights in the federal courts. As a result, Title IX is now less effective in protecting student survivors than it was a decade ago. And in some ways, Title IX now effectively encourages schools to mistreat victims. What a bitter irony for a sex discrimination law.

Some of these changes, such as the Trump…
items.t: To combat sexual assault on campus, it’s time to look past Title IX

Change is coming to Washington, DC, next Congress — and one Democratic senator thinks that that should also mean a change in leadership for the new Senate majority.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY), who has led the party’s caucus in the upper chamber for a decade, for the top job in the new Congress. In an interview on Vox’s America, Actually podcast, Van Hollen told host Astead Herndon that Schumer has been too timid in confronting Trump and the Republican Party, and too unwilling to use unconventional means to try to rally support for Democratic causes.

“My view is that working outside the Congress to highlight the attacks on our democracy was essential. You can’t just use the same tools that were used before Trump to take on a lawless Trump,” Van Hollen said. “We need to organize in this moment to help protect our democracy and our Constitution and get things done and deliver.”

items.title: Millions of turkeys will be thrown in the trash this Thanksgiving
items.summary:
A turkey arrives at the 2024 White House turkey pardon, a strange annual “song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them,” as Vox’s Kenny Torrella put it last year. | Susan Walsh/Associated Press 

This week, tens of millions of Americans will partake in a national ritual many of us say we don’t especially enjoy or find meaning in. We will collectively eat tens of millions of turkeys , factory-farmed and heavily engineered animals that bear scant resemblance to the wild birds that have been apocryphally written into the Thanksgiving story. (The first Thanksgiving probably didn’t have turkey.) And we will do it all even though turkey meat is widely considered flavorless and unpalatable. 

“It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout,” journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice . “Deep down, we know this, but bury it beneath happy memories of Thanksgivings past.” 

So what is essentially the national holiday of meat-eating revolves around an animal dish that no one really likes. That fact clashes with the widely accepted answer to the central question of why it’s so hard to convince everyone to ditch meat , or even to eat less of it: the taste, stupid. 

Undoubtedly, that has something to do with it. But I think the real answer is a lot more complicated, and the tasteless Thanksgiving turkey explains why.

• Why Americans eat turkey on Thanksgiving, despite many of us not liking it very much! 

• What life is like for a Thanksgiving…
items.t: Millions of turkeys will be thrown in the trash this Thanksgiving

items.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
items.summary:
By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life,…
items.t: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar

items.title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
items.summary:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

items.title: The Supreme Court is about to decide if assault rifle bans can exist
items.summary:
Activists rally outside the Supreme Court before a Second Amendment case in 2023. | ﻿Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images 

On December 2, the Supreme Court will hear two cases asking whether lawmakers may ban so-called assault rifles, semiautomatic weapons equipped with various features that allow a shooter to fire many rounds with greater accuracy than if they used an ordinary rifle.

The cases involve two similar laws, one out of Cook County, Illinois and another out of Connecticut, that seek to ban civilian ownership of AR-15s, a popular gun that was used in several recent mass shootings, and similar weapons. While there are subtle differences between the two laws, both ban semiautomatic rifles with features such as pistol grips that reduce recoil and make it easier for a shooter to rapidly fire many shots at a target.

(There is a chance that the Cook County case will be declared moot , but if that happens the Court will still be able to decide the Connecticut case.)

The most striking thing about the briefs in these two cases, Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins , is that they describe two entirely different Second Amendments that operate in completely different ways. Yet both of these competing Second Amendments can be found in this Court’s precedents.

It’s unclear just how much the Court’s decision to choose one Second Amendment over the other will matter to future cases, because the Court sometimes reaches results in gun rights cases that are difficult to justify under any of its previous precedents — the most consistent pattern in this…
items.t: The Supreme Court is about to decide if assault rifle bans can exist

items.title: How to politely opt out of obligatory gift giving this season
items.summary:
You don’t need me to tell you it’s expensive out there — groceries and gas cost a fortune, inflation is still hot hot hot , and getting a raise? Maybe next year, babe. 

If this is relatable for you, you might be dreading the holidays. Maybe not the celebrations, exactly, but the gift giving of it all — all the spending, all the stuff. Between the cost to your bank account and the cost to the planet, I wouldn’t blame you if the thought of holiday gifting was causing some angst right now. 

“The holidays are already stressful. Even if we think they’re fun, there’s a lot of stress associated with it,” financial therapist Lindsay Bryan-Podvin tells Vox. With higher prices on gas, groceries, travel, and eating out, “it’s compounding.”

It doesn’t have to be torturous, though. With the right approach, you can get your loved ones on board with a lower-cost, lower-waste holiday season. It just takes creativity and a little finesse.

Set your budget for gifts 

So, you know you want to do things differently this season but you’re still planning to do some gifting. The first step? Make a budget, Bryan-Podvin says.

A pro tip for next year 

Once you get through the chaos of this season, think about setting up a budget for gifting in January or February. 

Bryan-Podvin has a sinking fund called “Gifts” that she adds to every month. When a gifting occasion hits, she looks to that account to see how much she can afford to spend. 

“Whatever’s in there helps direct how much I will or won’t spend,” she says.

To set this up, see if your savings account offers a “bucketing” feature — a…

items.title: Why you should be skeptical of “responsible” seafood
items.summary:
Salmon labeled as “responsibly sourced” at a grocery store in Minnesota. | Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images 

This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare. 

Seafood is sort of having a moment. 

Influencers are talking up the benefits of tinned sardines , dry-aged fish is all the rage in fine dining, the poke bowl trend of the 2010s is still going strong, and “caviar bumps” are a thing.

These dishes may be getting much of the media attention, though it’s staples like bagged shrimp and filets of salmon or tuna that usually end up in shoppers’ carts. While seafood makes up a small share of the typical US diet on balance, it’s been slowly increasing over the past few decades. Now, everyone from the Trump administration to the World Economic Forum to major environmental groups wants to accelerate this trend and put more seafood at the center of the plate. And they want a lot of that fish to come not from the ocean but from farms. 

Fish farming, also known as aquaculture, is often touted as a more sustainable alternative to wild-caught fish — a way to give oceans a break after centuries of heavy exploitation . And so it’s not uncommon to see claims like “sustainably farmed” and “responsibly raised” on packages of farm-raised salmon or shrimp. 

Key takeaways 

More than half of the world’s seafood now comes from farms, and a lot of farmed fish is marketed as “responsibly raised” or “sustainably farmed.” 

Two nonprofits analyzed these types of marketing claims on over 300 seafood…
items.t: Your “responsible” seafood isn’t what it seems

items.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams
items.summary:
By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

Continue reading...
items.t: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams

items.title: Why Trump saved Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Donald Trump greets Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is personally intervening to keep the AI industry afloat. 

What happened? Jensen Huang, the recently ousted Nvidia CEO, is back atop the company as of Monday morning, after Trump dialed into an Nvidia board meeting over the weekend to offer “assurance” about legal and national security concerns around Huang. 

Huang’s restoration — after he resigned following reports about multiple alleged affairs, including one with a possible Chinese spy — is a remarkable reversal of fortune. It also marks an unprecedented, at least in the modern era, level of direct White House interference with corporate America.

What’s the context? This is the outcome that Trump, Elon Musk, and many of his other allies on the tech right have been agitating for since Huang stepped down not even two weeks ago. 

As head of Nvidia, Huang has become — apparently quite literally — the AI industry’s “indispensable man.” In addition to being the leading maker of advanced AI chips, Nvidia is sometimes referred to as the “central bank of AI” for the financing schemes it uses to keep major labs afloat. That gives it a great deal of sway over better-known companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. 

Huang, by some in the industry and on Wall Street, was…

Huang, the ex-ex-Nvidia CEO, is officially back at the helm of the giant chipmaker he cofounded 35 years ago — and all his past indiscretions have been forgiven, if still under investigation. And the stock market loves it , with investors joining Trump in betting that Huang’s singular business talents will make up for the considerable chaos he’s personally caused already.

items.title: Jensen Huang is back. It might not last.
items.summary:
A television broadcasts Nvidia news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) on November 23, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty 

For a brief moment after the 2026 midterms, it had seemed that President Donald Trump was a true lame duck already.

First came Democrats’ blue tsunami, a popular rejection of his record by voters that threatens to constrain much of his agenda. Then there was the ouster of Jensen Huang , a celebrity CEO who had been deeply influential on the Trump administration’s AI and chip policy, to bipartisan chagrin , and was arguably the single most important private individual in the broader economy . 

Huang’s downfall came after allegations that he had affairs with two employees as well as a tech executive who some US officials thought was a Chinese spy . And it seemed to signify that the era in which Trump and the tech right — a group of wealthy venture capitalists and CEOs who backed Trump, such as Elon Musk and David Sacks — ran the country was over.

Not so fast. Just 11 days after Huang resigned, Nvidia made the shocking announcement Monday that it was putting him back in the CEO job.

And the company did so after a very public campaign from leading tech right figures and Trump . The president reportedly called into Nvidia’s board meeting as the company weighed Huang’s return, and in a CNBC interview Monday, Trump referred to the outcome as a “deal” that he’d made. “I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them,” he said . 

In their own announcement, Nvidia indicated that the White House assured them Huang…

items.title: PNG’s parliament is voting on ratifying Bougainville independence. A ‘no’ won’t be the end of the story

An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process.

In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result.

A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving.

Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track.

items.title: Democrats’ tantalizing dream of a Blue Utah
items.summary:
An American flag hangs in Orem, Utah, while the Orem Utah Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints rises in the background. | Charles-McClintock Wilson/Getty Images 

If someone asked which shift or flip was most surprising in this year’s blue tsunami, you might be hard-pressed to choose. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator in nearly a century. Republicans lost every statewide race in Texas. With Democrats winning in South Carolina and Mississippi, conventional wisdom about what counts as a battleground went completely out the window.

And then there’s Utah.

A state that last voted for a Democratic presidential candidate in 1964; a bastion of cultural conservatism and business-friendly politics; the home of Mitt Romney and the Mormon church . And now…although a handful of votes are still waiting to be counted, it looks like, for the first time in decades, more votes were cast for Democrats than Republicans in Utah this cycle.

Is this just another high spot for a fluke blue wave — or a pivot in American political history?

For Democrats, the results have led to some improbable dreams about “Blutah,” a middle-of-the-nation state that, like Colorado, could be swinging from a GOP stronghold into a Democratic opportunity. It’s not yet clear how likely that is; there was no galvanizing statewide race on the Utah ballot this year, and registered Republicans still dramatically outnumber Democrats. The 2026 results could just be a phenomenon of a blue-wave midterm year, where the absence of a presidential contest left more Republican-friendly voters at…
items.t: Democrats’ tantalizing dream of a Blue Utah

items.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
items.summary:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.

items.title: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?
items.summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year.

Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits.

The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks.

Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal.

Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI,…
items.t: Was Anthropic’s record US$81 billion listing a vote of confidence in AI – and what’s next?
